claim: Granulomas are defined by the presence of organized layers of immune cells that include macrophages.
source: Granulomas are defined by the presence of organized layers of immune cells that include macrophages.
evidence: This is a definitional statement cited from the literature (Warren, 1976) as indicated in the introduction.

claim: Chromobacterium violaceum induces the innate immune system to form granulomas in the liver in a mouse infection model.
source: We recently established a mouse infection model where Chromobacterium violaceum induces the innate immune system to form granulomas in the liver.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' recent work (Harvest et al., 2023).

claim: The granuloma response successfully eradicates C. violaceum bacteria and returns the liver to homeostasis.
source: This response successfully eradicates the bacteria and returns the liver to homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the authors' infection model.

claim: Ccr2–/– mice had negligible numbers of macrophages in C. violaceum-infected lesions.
source: Ccr2–/– mice had negligible numbers of macrophages, but large numbers of neutrophils, in the C. violaceum-infected lesions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments with Ccr2–/– mice as shown in Figure 6 and Figure 7.

claim: Ccr2–/– mice had large numbers of neutrophils in C. violaceum-infected lesions.
source: Ccr2–/– mice had negligible numbers of macrophages, but large numbers of neutrophils, in the C. violaceum-infected lesions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments with Ccr2–/– mice as shown in Figure 6.

claim: Lesions in Ccr2–/– mice had abnormal architecture resulting in loss of bacterial containment.
source: In addition, lesions had abnormal architecture resulting in loss of bacterial containment.
evidence: This is observed through histological analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Without CCR2, C. violaceum bacteria disseminated and mice succumbed to infection.
source: Without CCR2, bacteria disseminated and the mice succumbed to the infection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival curves and CFU data in Figure 6.

claim: Macrophages are critical to form a successful innate granuloma in response to C. violaceum.
source: This indicates that macrophages are critical to form a successful innate granuloma in response to C. violaceum.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the Ccr2–/– mouse experiments showing loss of macrophages leads to infection failure.

claim: C. violaceum only causes morbidity and mortality in immunocompromised animals or individuals.
source: Chromobacterium violaceum is one such pathogen that invades host cells and replicates in the intracellular niche, but only causes morbidity and mortality in immunocompromised animals or individuals (Macher, 1982).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Macher, 1982).

claim: Wildtype C57BL/6 mice develop necrotic liver granulomas in response to C. violaceum infection.
source: We discovered that during infection, wildtype (WT) C57BL/6 mice develop necrotic liver granulomas in response to this ubiquitous soil microbe (Harvest et al., 2023; Maltez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a discovery from the authors' previous work.

claim: Liver microabscesses can be macroscopically visualized as soon as 1 day post-infection with C. violaceum.
source: As soon as 1 day post-infection (1 DPI), liver microabscesses can be macroscopically visualized.
evidence: This is an observation from the infection model.

claim: Lesions are composed primarily of neutrophils until approximately 3–5 DPI during C. violaceum infection.
source: These lesions are composed primarily of neutrophils until approximately 3–5 DPI, when, importantly, monocytes traffic into the area and form a mature granuloma starting at 5 DPI.
evidence: This is a temporal observation from the infection model.

claim: Monocytes traffic into infected areas and form a mature granuloma starting at 5 DPI during C. violaceum infection.
source: These lesions are composed primarily of neutrophils until approximately 3–5 DPI, when, importantly, monocytes traffic into the area and form a mature granuloma starting at 5 DPI.
evidence: This is a temporal observation from the infection model.

claim: Bacterial burdens begin to decrease once the macrophage zone surrounds the infected lesion.
source: Once the resulting macrophage zone surrounds the infected lesion, bacterial burdens begin to decrease, suggesting that granuloma macrophages are an important cell type for the clearance of C. violaceum.
evidence: This correlation is observed in the infection model data.

claim: By 21 DPI, virtually all mice clear C. violaceum infection and resolve granuloma pathology.
source: By 21 DPI, virtually all mice clear the infection and resolve the granuloma pathology, leaving small collagen scars in place of lesions (Harvest et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the infection model.

claim: Spatial transcriptomics was used to investigate the spatial and temporal expression of all CC and CXC chemokines and their receptors within the granuloma response.
source: We use spatial transcriptomics to investigate the spatial and temporal expression of all CC and CXC chemokines and their receptors within this granuloma response.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The spatial transcriptomics dataset identified 16 unique clusters with differentially expressed genes.
source: the dataset successfully identified 16 unique clusters with differentially expressed genes (Figure 1B), representing cell types (e.g. hepatocytes and endothelial cells), and also representing spatial elements (e.g. necrotic core center, etc.).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: 10 DPI was the most enriched timepoint with all seven non-hepatocyte clusters present.
source: 10 DPI was the most enriched timepoint with all seven non-hepatocyte clusters present (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cxcl1 and Cxcl2 show high expression levels as early as 12 hr post-infection (0.5 DPI).
source: We observed high expression levels of chemokines involved in neutrophil trafficking (e.g. Cxcl1 and Cxcl2) as early as 12 hr post-infection (0.5 DPI) (Figure 2A, B), which correlates with our previous data that neutrophils are the first immune cells to arrive in response to C. violaceum (Harvest et al., 2023).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A, B and correlates with previous findings.

claim: Cxcl3 and Cxcl5 show delayed expression peaking around 10 DPI.
source: In contrast to Cxcl1 and Cxcl2, Cxcl3, and Cxcl5 show delayed expression peaking around 10 DPI (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: At 5 DPI, Cxcl1 is expressed more toward the periphery of the lesion, while Cxcl2 is expressed more toward the center.
source: For example, at 5 DPI Cxcl1 is expressed more toward the periphery of the lesion, while Cxcl2 is expressed more toward the center (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This spatial difference is shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: Expression of CXCR2 ligands is absent by 21 DPI, which correlates with the time at which the majority of mice clear the infection.
source: For all of these ligands, expression is absent by 21 DPI, which correlates with the time at which the majority of mice clear the infection.
evidence: This correlation is observed in the spatial transcriptomics data.

claim: Ccl2 was the most highly upregulated CCR2 ligand during C. violaceum infection.
source: Ccl2 was the most highly upregulated, while Ccl12 was expressed only at low levels, and Ccl7 expression was somewhere in between (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Ccl12 was expressed only at low levels during C. violaceum infection.
source: Ccl2 was the most highly upregulated, while Ccl12 was expressed only at low levels, and Ccl7 expression was somewhere in between (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: CCR2 ligands are not expressed by 21 DPI during C. violaceum infection.
source: Similar to the chemokines involved in neutrophil trafficking, these ligands are not expressed by 21 DPI.
evidence: This is observed in the spatial transcriptomics data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The adaptive immune response is dispensable to successfully form granulomas around and eradicate C. violaceum.
source: In our previous studies, we showed that the adaptive immune response is dispensable to successfully form granulomas around, and then to eradicate, C. violaceum (Harvest et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: Several chemokines involved in T cell trafficking are absent or only expressed at low levels during C. violaceum infection.
source: In agreement with those findings, several chemokines involved in T cell trafficking are absent or only expressed at low levels (i.e. Cxcl11, Ccl1, Ccl22, and Ccl25) (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A, B and agrees with previous findings about adaptive immunity.

claim: Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 are highly expressed during the first few days of C. violaceum infection.
source: On the other hand, other chemokines involved in T cell trafficking such as Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 are highly expressed during the first few days of infection, as is their receptor Cxcr3 (Figure 4A, C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A, C.

claim: T cells are not recruited in large numbers during primary C. violaceum infection.
source: During primary infection, T cell recruitment is not essential for clearance and we found that T cells are not recruited in large numbers (Harvest et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: Basophils and eosinophils were not observed histologically during C. violaceum infection.
source: We did not observe basophils or eosinophils histologically during infection with C. violaceum, and this was again supported by the absence or low expression of chemokines involved in trafficking of these cell types (i.e. Ccl11, Ccl24, and Ccl26) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on histological observations and chemokine expression data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ccr3 is not expressed at any timepoint during C. violaceum infection.
source: During infection with C. violaceum, however, Ccr3 is not expressed at any timepoint (Figure 4D), further supporting that eosinophils are not involved in the granuloma response to C. violaceum.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cxcl13 is expressed at low levels during C. violaceum infection.
source: However, Cxcl13 is expressed at low levels, and Cxcr5 is absent in the C. violaceum model (Figure 4A, C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A, C.

claim: Cxcr5 is absent in the C. violaceum model.
source: However, Cxcl13 is expressed at low levels, and Cxcr5 is absent in the C. violaceum model (Figure 4A, C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A, C.

claim: Cxcl1 is highly expressed at 1 DPI during C. violaceum infection.
source: Furthermore, there are interesting differences in temporal expression; Cxcl1 is highly expressed at 1 DPI while Ccl2 expression peaks at 3 DPI (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ccl2 expression peaks at 3 DPI during C. violaceum infection.
source: Furthermore, there are interesting differences in temporal expression; Cxcl1 is highly expressed at 1 DPI while Ccl2 expression peaks at 3 DPI (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Neutrophils traffic to the liver within 1 DPI during C. violaceum infection.
source: Altogether, these data corroborate our previous findings that neutrophils traffic to the liver within 1 DPI, and monocytes traffic and form granulomas beginning at 3 DPI.
evidence: This is stated as corroboration of previous findings with the current data.

claim: Monocytes traffic and form granulomas beginning at 3 DPI during C. violaceum infection.
source: Altogether, these data corroborate our previous findings that neutrophils traffic to the liver within 1 DPI, and monocytes traffic and form granulomas beginning at 3 DPI.
evidence: This is stated as corroboration of previous findings with the current data.

claim: Ccr2–/– mice are highly susceptible to C. violaceum infection and succumb beginning at 5 DPI.
source: Strikingly, Ccr2–/– mice were highly susceptible and succumbed to infection beginning at 5 DPI, with all mice dying by 9 DPI (Figure 6A), which is more severe than the phenotype in Nos2–/– mice (Harvest et al., 2023).
evidence: This is shown in the survival curve in Figure 6A.

claim: All Ccr2–/– mice died by 9 DPI during C. violaceum infection.
source: Strikingly, Ccr2–/– mice were highly susceptible and succumbed to infection beginning at 5 DPI, with all mice dying by 9 DPI (Figure 6A), which is more severe than the phenotype in Nos2–/– mice (Harvest et al., 2023).
evidence: This is shown in the survival curve in Figure 6A.

claim: At 5 DPI, Ccr2–/– mice had increased liver burdens compared to WT mice.
source: At 5 DPI, Ccr2–/– mice had increased liver burdens (Figure 6B), and bacterial dissemination into the spleen (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At 5 DPI, Ccr2–/– mice had bacterial dissemination into the spleen.
source: At 5 DPI, Ccr2–/– mice had increased liver burdens (Figure 6B), and bacterial dissemination into the spleen (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ccr2–/– mice had abnormal lesions which were more numerous and larger than the lesions of WT mice.
source: We also observed that Ccr2–/– mice had abnormal lesions which were more numerous and larger than the lesions of WT mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Uninfected WT and uninfected Ccr2–/– mice had a similar frequency of macrophages in the liver.
source: Uninfected WT and uninfected Ccr2–/– mice had a similar frequency of macrophages in the liver (Figure 6F), likely representing the tissue-resident Kupffer cell population, as well as a similar frequency of splenic macrophages (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Upon infection, the livers of Ccr2–/– mice had markedly less macrophages compared to WT mice.
source: However, upon infection, the livers of Ccr2–/– mice had markedly less macrophages and drastically more neutrophils compared to the livers of WT mice (Figure 6F, G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Upon infection, the livers of Ccr2–/– mice had drastically more neutrophils compared to WT mice.
source: However, upon infection, the livers of Ccr2–/– mice had markedly less macrophages and drastically more neutrophils compared to the livers of WT mice (Figure 6F, G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Failure to recruit monocytes leads to enhanced neutrophil recruitment during C. violaceum infection.
source: This trend was also observed in the spleen (Figure 6H, I) and blood (Figure 6J, K), showing that failure to recruit monocytes leads to enhanced neutrophil recruitment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6H-K and is an inference from the data.

claim: Infected Ccr2–/– mice had slightly more macrophages in the liver, spleen, and blood compared to uninfected Ccr2–/– mice.
source: Interestingly, infected Ccr2–/– mice did have slightly more macrophages in the liver, spleen, and blood compared to uninfected Ccr2–/– mice (Figure 6F, H, J), suggesting that loss of CCR2 does not completely abrogate monocyte recruitment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F, H, J.

claim: By 5 DPI, all three zones (necrotic core, coagulative necrosis, and macrophage zone) are distinctly visible through H&E staining in WT mice.
source: By 5 DPI, all three layers are distinctly visible through H&E staining (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: C. violaceum is contained within the necrotic core in WT mice at 5 DPI.
source: Furthermore, we consistently see containment of C. violaceum within the necrotic core (Figure 7B), which overlaps with pronounced Ly6G staining (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: By 5 DPI, the macrophage zone is clearly visible in WT mice, showing that macrophages surround the granuloma.
source: Importantly, by 5 DPI the macrophage zone is clearly visible in WT mice, showing that macrophages surround the granuloma and form a protective zone between the coagulative necrosis zone and healthy hepatocytes outside the infected lesion (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Lesions in Ccr2–/– mice lack distinct zones compared to WT mice.
source: Compared to WT mice, lesions in Ccr2–/– mice lack these distinct zones.
evidence: This is observed through histological comparison in Figure 7.

claim: The coagulative necrosis zone was largely absent from most lesions in Ccr2–/– mice.
source: Though Ccr2–/– mice had larger areas of necrotic debris, the coagulative necrosis zone was largely absent from most lesions (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Clotting was more abundant in Ccr2–/– mice compared to WT mice during C. violaceum infection.
source: In previous studies, we also observed sporadic clotting in WT mice (Harvest et al., 2023), and this clotting was even more abundant in Ccr2–/– mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lesions in Ccr2–/– mice had abnormal budding morphology that stained strongly for C. violaceum.
source: Strikingly, lesions in Ccr2–/– mice had abnormal budding morphology, which stained very strongly for C. violaceum (Figure 7F) and Ly6G neutrophils (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F.

claim: An organized macrophage zone was absent from the majority of lesions in Ccr2–/– mice.
source: Though we were able to visualize the Kupffer cell population scattered throughout the liver, an organized macrophage zone was absent from the majority of lesions in Ccr2–/– mice (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Without distinct coagulative necrosis or macrophage zones, C. violaceum staining extends well outside the center of each lesion in Ccr2–/– mice.
source: Importantly, without distinct coagulative necrosis or macrophage zones, C. violaceum staining extends well outside the center of each lesion.
evidence: This is observed in the histological analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Numerous bacteria were identified in immune cells immediately adjacent to the healthy hepatocyte layer in Ccr2–/– mice.
source: In fact, numerous bacteria were identified in immune cells immediately adjacent to the healthy hepatocyte layer (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Ccr2–/– mice produce higher amounts of CCL2 in the liver and serum compared to WT mice at 3 DPI.
source: Furthermore, immunofluorescent staining of CCL2 revealed diffuse quantities in both WT and Ccr2–/– mice, with Ccr2–/– mice producing higher amounts of CCL2 in the liver and serum compared to WT mice at 3 DPI (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Despite excessive numbers of neutrophils, Ccr2–/– mice are unable to clear C. violaceum infection.
source: Despite the excessive number of neutrophils in the liver, spleen, and blood of Ccr2–/– mice (Figure 6G, I, K), these mice are unable to clear the infection and ultimately succumb.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 survival and CFU data.

claim: Casp1::Casp11 DKO and Gsdmd–/– mice have abnormal lesion architecture with budding morphology and loss of bacterial containment similar to Ccr2–/– mice.
source: Previously, we observed abnormal lesion architecture in Casp1::Casp11 DKO and Gsdmd–/– mice with budding morphology and loss of bacterial containment (Harvest et al., 2023) that is remarkably similar to the architecture observed in Ccr2–/– mice (Figure 7F).
evidence: This comparison is made with previous work cited (Harvest et al., 2023) and shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Macrophage recruitment and pyroptosis are both essential in defense against and containment of C. violaceum.
source: Together, these data suggest that macrophage recruitment and pyroptosis are both essential in defense against, and containment of, C. violaceum.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing Ccr2–/– mice with previous pyroptosis-deficient mouse data.

claim: Without monocytes trafficking to the site of infection, C. violaceum is able to replicate and spread into adjacent hepatocytes.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that without monocytes trafficking to the site of infection, C. violaceum is able to replicate and spread into adjacent hepatocytes, resulting in ever-expanding lesions.
evidence: This is inferred from the Ccr2–/– mouse data showing loss of containment and increased bacterial burdens.

claim: Macrophages are essential for clearance of C. violaceum from the infected liver.
source: Here, we demonstrate that macrophages are essential for clearance of C. violaceum from the infected liver, and for protection against dissemination into the spleen.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the Ccr2–/– mouse experiments.

claim: Loss of CCR2-dependent monocyte trafficking results in a loss of bacterial containment during C. violaceum infection.
source: Loss of CCR2-dependent monocyte trafficking results in a loss of bacterial containment, ultimately leading to uncontrolled bacterial replication in the liver, evidenced by elevated CFU burdens and increased lesion size.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the Ccr2–/– mouse experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Tissue-resident Kupffer cells and infected hepatocytes are likely the first cells to sound the alarm during C. violaceum infection.
source: It is likely that the tissue-resident Kupffer cells and infected hepatocytes are the first cells to sound the alarm, calling for neutrophils.
evidence: This is speculation based on the infection model observations.

claim: Initial recruitment of neutrophils during C. violaceum infection likely involves chemokines redundantly with other chemoattractants.
source: The initial recruitment of neutrophils likely involves chemokines (i.e. CXCL1 and CXCL2) redundantly with other chemoattractants such as formylated peptides and leukotrienes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the literature and the observation that CXCR2 inhibition was not fully effective.

claim: CCR2 is an essential chemokine receptor for monocyte trafficking in response to C. violaceum.
source: Based on our data, CCR2 is an essential chemokine receptor for monocyte trafficking in response to C. violaceum, but we have not yet determined which ligand(s) mediate this response.
evidence: This is concluded from the Ccr2–/– mouse experiments.

claim: CCL2 may be a critical chemokine that promotes monocyte recruitment in response to C. violaceum.
source: In agreement, we see upregulation of Ccl2 in several clusters and deposition of CCL2 protein in wide areas around granulomas, further suggesting that CCL2 may be a critical chemokine that promotes monocyte recruitment in response to C. violaceum.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial transcriptomics and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Ccl7 is expressed by fewer clusters and to a lesser degree compared to Ccl2, with slightly delayed expression.
source: In contrast, Ccl7 is expressed by fewer clusters, and to a lesser degree, and its expression is slightly delayed compared to Ccl2.
evidence: This is observed in the spatial transcriptomics data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The small population of macrophages in Ccr2–/– mice is not sufficient to protect against C. violaceum infection.
source: Regardless, this small population of macrophages is not sufficient to protect against infection with C. violaceum.
evidence: This is concluded from the survival and CFU data in Ccr2–/– mice.

claim: Loss of CCR2 during Y. pseudotuberculosis infection enhances clearance.
source: Loss of CCR2-dependent monocyte trafficking enhances clearance of Y. pseudotuberculosis (Zhang et al., 2018), which is a surprising result as typically macrophages would be expected to be important to clear infections.
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Zhang et al., 2018).

claim: The role of CCR2 during M. tuberculosis infection is strain-dependent and varies depending on dose and route of infection.
source: The role of CCR2 during M. tuberculosis infection is strain-dependent, and also varies depending on the dose and route of infection (Dunlap et al., 2018; Peters et al., 2001; Scott and Flynn, 2002).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Expression of specific chemokines in response to M. tuberculosis differs from those observed in response to C. violaceum.
source: For example, expression of specific chemokines in response to M. tuberculosis differs from those we observe in response to C. violaceum, especially chemokines that attract T cells (Kang et al., 2011).
evidence: This comparison is made with published literature (Kang et al., 2011).

claim: M. tuberculosis bacterial burdens plateau at 21 DPI.
source: Importantly, while M. tuberculosis bacterial burdens plateau at 21 DPI, almost all mice clear C. violaceum by this timepoint.
evidence: This comparison is made with M. tuberculosis literature.

claim: Almost all mice clear C. violaceum by 21 DPI.
source: Importantly, while M. tuberculosis bacterial burdens plateau at 21 DPI, almost all mice clear C. violaceum by this timepoint.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the infection model.

claim: C. violaceum appears to lack sufficient virulence factors to enable it to replicate within macrophages.
source: In contrast, C. violaceum appears to lack sufficient virulence factors to enable it to replicate within macrophages (Batista and da Silva Neto, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Batista and da Silva Neto, 2017).

claim: Neutrophil recruitment wanes as the granuloma matures in WT mice during C. violaceum infection.
source: In WT mice, neutrophil recruitment wanes as the granuloma matures, which coincides with clearance of C. violaceum.
evidence: This is observed in the infection model data.

claim: In Ccr2–/– mice, elevated neutrophil numbers are seen at 5 DPI, suggesting continuous recruitment in the absence of macrophages.
source: However, in the Ccr2–/– mice, we see elevated neutrophil numbers at 5 DPI, suggesting that neutrophils are continuously recruited in the absence of macrophages.
evidence: This is observed in the flow cytometry data in Figure 6.

claim: CCR1 and CCR5 differentially affected monocyte localization within a transwell system in vitro.
source: In vitro studies found that CCR1 and CCR5 differentially affected monocyte localization within a transwell system, implying that a system exists for fine-tuning the exact location of macrophages within inflamed tissues (Shi and Pamer, 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Shi and Pamer, 2011).

claim: CCR1 and CCR5 are highly upregulated in the C. violaceum-induced granuloma.
source: These receptors are highly upregulated in the C. violaceum-induced granuloma and are thus good candidates for balancing the localization of macrophages between the coagulative necrosis zone and healthy tissue outside the granuloma.
evidence: This is observed in the spatial transcriptomics data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Nitration of CCL2 and CCL3 by peroxynitrite reduces monocyte and neutrophil chemotaxis, respectively.
source: For example, nitration of CCL2 and CCL3 by peroxynitrite was shown to reduce monocyte and neutrophil chemotaxis, respectively (Sato et al., 1999; Sato et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: MMP-2 cleaves both CXCL12 and CCL7, abolishing their ability to induce chemotaxis.
source: For example, MMP-2 cleaves both CXCL12 and CCL7, abolishing their ability to induce chemotaxis (McQuibban et al., 2000; McQuibban et al., 2001); importantly, all three of these genes are upregulated during C. violaceum infection (Table 1, Table 3, Table 4).
evidence: This is cited from published literature and correlated with the current data.

claim: MMP-2, MMP-9, CXCL12, and CCL7 are all upregulated during C. violaceum infection.
source: For example, MMP-2 cleaves both CXCL12 and CCL7, abolishing their ability to induce chemotaxis (McQuibban et al., 2000; McQuibban et al., 2001); importantly, all three of these genes are upregulated during C. violaceum infection (Table 1, Table 3, Table 4).
evidence: This is shown in Tables 1, 3, and 4.

claim: MMP-2 and MMP-9 are important to limit tissue damage in lung inflammation.
source: Furthermore, MMP-2 and MMP-9 have been extensively studied in the context of lung inflammation, both of which are important to limit tissue damage (Greenlee et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Greenlee et al., 2006).

claim: MMP-9 promotes or inhibits liver fibrosis and wound repair depending on the context.
source: MMP-9 has also been shown to promote or inhibit liver fibrosis and wound repair, depending on the context (Feng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Feng et al., 2018).

claim: Spatial transcriptomics was performed using the 10x Genomics Visium Platform.
source: Spatial data were generated in Harvest et al., 2023 using the 10X Genomics Visium Platform.
evidence: This describes the methodology used.

claim: The sctransform method was used to normalize spatial transcriptomics data.
source: To account for cell-to-cell variation, especially across tissues, pre-processing included normalization using sctransform (Hafemeister and Satija, 2019).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology.

claim: Ccr2RFP mice lack functional CCR2.
source: Ccr2RFP mice (referred to as Ccr2–/–; originally generated in Saederup et al., 2010)
evidence: The notation Ccr2–/– indicates these are knockout mice lacking functional CCR2.

claim: Reparixin is an allosteric inhibitor of CXCR1 and CXCR2.
source: Reparixin is an allosteric inhibitor of CXCR1 and CXCR2 that has been shown to inhibit neutrophil trafficking during ischemia–reperfusion injury and acid-induced acute lung injury (Bertini et al., 2004; Zarbock et al., 2008; Hosoki and Sur, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Reparixin treatment did not significantly affect bacterial burdens in the liver at 3 DPI.
source: Though there was no difference in CFU for the liver, a few CFU were recovered from the spleens of two reparixin-treated mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which, though this was not statistically significant, is unusual for WT mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Reparixin was poorly soluble in PBS.
source: In our hands, reparixin was poorly soluble in PBS, which could account for some of the variability.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Reparixin was not a successful inhibitor of neutrophil recruitment during C. violaceum infection.
source: Altogether, it is clear that reparixin was not a successful inhibitor of neutrophil recruitment during infection with C. violaceum.
evidence: This is concluded from the reparixin experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: FPR2 promotes neutrophil migration in response to bacterial infection in the liver.
source: Importantly, formyl peptide receptors (FPRs) such as FPR2 promote neutrophil migration in response to bacterial infection in the liver (Lee et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Lee et al., 2023).

claim: FPRs are upregulated during C. violaceum infection.
source: In support of this, FPRs are upregulated in this model (Table 3).
evidence: This is shown in Table 3.

claim: The appearance of organized macrophages at approximately 5 DPI correlates with a subsequent decrease in bacterial burdens.
source: Previously, we noticed that the appearance of organized macrophages at approximately 5 DPI correlates with a subsequent decrease in bacterial burdens (Harvest et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: Nos2–/– mice succumb to C. violaceum infection beginning at 7 DPI.
source: We also observed that Nos2–/– mice, which lack the ability to express inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), succumb to infection beginning at 7 DPI, a timepoint when the granuloma matures with a thicker macrophage ring (Harvest et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: Ccr2–/– mice have intact tissue-resident macrophage populations.
source: Importantly, Ccr2–/– mice have intact tissue-resident macrophage populations but are unable to recruit additional monocytes in the event of infection (Kurihara et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Kurihara et al., 1997).

claim: Ccr2–/– mice are unable to recruit additional monocytes in the event of infection.
source: Importantly, Ccr2–/– mice have intact tissue-resident macrophage populations but are unable to recruit additional monocytes in the event of infection (Kurihara et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Kurihara et al., 1997).

claim: The phenotype of Ccr2–/– mice during C. violaceum infection is more severe than the phenotype in Nos2–/– mice.
source: Strikingly, Ccr2–/– mice were highly susceptible and succumbed to infection beginning at 5 DPI, with all mice dying by 9 DPI (Figure 6A), which is more severe than the phenotype in Nos2–/– mice (Harvest et al., 2023).
evidence: This comparison is made with previous work on Nos2–/– mice.

claim: Deletion of Ccr2 has the opposite phenotype during Y. pseudotuberculosis infection compared to C. violaceum infection.
source: This is in contrast to Yersinia pseudotuberculosis models in which deletion of Ccr2 has the opposite phenotype, and loss of monocytes is actually protective (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This comparison is made with published literature (Zhang et al., 2018).

claim: Loss of Ccr2 has no effect on survival in some M. tuberculosis infection contexts.
source: This also contrasts with M. tuberculosis models where loss of Ccr2 has no effect on survival in some contexts (Domingo-Gonzalez et al., 2016; Scott and Flynn, 2002).
evidence: This comparison is made with published literature.

claim: CD4+ Th1 cells are required to stimulate antibacterial activity of macrophages in M. tuberculosis-induced granulomas.
source: It is a curious observation that T cells are dispensable during primary infection because in Mycobacterium tuberculosis-induced granulomas, CD4+ T helper type 1 (Th1) cells are required to stimulate the antibacterial activity of macrophages (Pagán and Ramakrishnan, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Pagán and Ramakrishnan, 2018).

claim: M. tuberculosis is able to intracellularly infect macrophages.
source: A key difference between granuloma formation in response to C. violaceum compared to M. tuberculosis could be that M. tuberculosis is able to intracellularly infect macrophages, whereas C. violaceum is unable to circumvent pyroptosis of macrophages.
evidence: This is stated as a known difference between the two pathogens.

claim: C. violaceum is unable to circumvent pyroptosis of macrophages.
source: A key difference between granuloma formation in response to C. violaceum compared to M. tuberculosis could be that M. tuberculosis is able to intracellularly infect macrophages, whereas C. violaceum is unable to circumvent pyroptosis of macrophages.
evidence: This is inferred from the authors' previous work on pyroptosis.

claim: The Ccr2–/– mice survive a few days longer than Casp1::Casp11 DKO and Gsdmd–/– mice and thus develop even larger lesions over time.
source: However, the Ccr2–/– mice survive a few days longer and thus develop even larger lesions over time.
evidence: This comparison is made with previous work on pyroptosis-deficient mice.

claim: The timeframe of Ccr2–/– mouse mortality is similar to that seen with Nos2–/– mice.
source: In addition, because the Ccr2–/– mice succumb in a timeframe similar to that seen with Nos2–/– mice, this supports our hypothesis that it is nitric oxide derived from granuloma macrophages that is specifically required for bacterial clearance.
evidence: This comparison is made with previous work on Nos2–/– mice.

claim: Nitric oxide derived from granuloma macrophages is specifically required for bacterial clearance of C. violaceum.
source: In addition, because the Ccr2–/– mice succumb in a timeframe similar to that seen with Nos2–/– mice, this supports our hypothesis that it is nitric oxide derived from granuloma macrophages that is specifically required for bacterial clearance.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by comparing Ccr2–/– and Nos2–/– mouse phenotypes.

claim: Upregulated genes, specifically chemokines, are critical to the formation of the granuloma in response to C. violaceum.
source: These in vivo data support the transcriptomics dataset and provide proof-of-concept that upregulated genes, specifically chemokines, are critical to the formation of the granuloma.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined transcriptomics and Ccr2–/– mouse data.

claim: Approximately 50 chemokines are now appreciated for their role in cellular chemotaxis.
source: Since their discovery in the 1980s, approximately 50 chemokines are now appreciated for their role in cellular chemotaxis (Zlotnik and Yoshie, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Zlotnik and Yoshie, 2012).

claim: Dysregulation of chemokine systems is linked to many diseases.
source: The temporal and spatial expression of chemokines and chemokine receptors dictate cellular trafficking, and dysregulation of these systems is linked to many diseases (Turner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Turner et al., 2014).

claim: Chemokines are categorized into four subfamilies based on the arrangement of N-terminal cysteines: CXC, CC, XC, and CX3C.
source: Chemokines have conserved cysteine residues, and the current naming system categorizes four subfamilies based on the arrangement of these N-terminal cysteines: CXC, CC, XC, and CX3C (Zlotnik and Yoshie, 2000).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Zlotnik and Yoshie, 2000).

claim: Inflammatory chemokines are rapidly upregulated in the presence of infection or other inflammatory stimuli.
source: Inflammatory chemokines are those that are rapidly upregulated in the presence of infection or other inflammatory stimuli (David and Kubes, 2019).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (David and Kubes, 2019).

claim: Chemokines contribute to wound healing and resolution of inflammation.
source: Lastly, it is now appreciated that chemokines also contribute to wound healing and resolution of inflammation, with coordinated efforts between neutrophils and macrophages to clean up debris and halt immune cell infiltration (Soehnlein and Lindbom, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Soehnlein and Lindbom, 2010).

claim: Neutrophils respond to chemotactic molecules in a hierarchical manner.
source: In fact, neutrophils respond to chemotactic molecules in a hierarchical manner, integrating a variety of signals and prioritizing end-target molecules (David and Kubes, 2019; Kolaczkowska and Kubes, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Adhesion molecules are required for transmigration of cells out of the blood and into tissues.
source: Further demonstrating the complexity of chemotaxis, various adhesion molecules are also required for transmigration of cells out of the blood and into tissues.
evidence: This is general knowledge about immune cell trafficking.

claim: Many chemokines, chemokine receptors, and adhesion molecules appear in the top twenty upregulated genes in several clusters during C. violaceum infection.
source: Indeed, we saw significant upregulation of a number of these genes in this model (Table 3), with many chemokines, chemokine receptors, and adhesion molecules appearing in the top twenty upregulated genes in several clusters (Table 4).
evidence: This is shown in Tables 3 and 4.

claim: Granulomas that form in response to M. tuberculosis often contain follicular dendritic cells which secrete CXCL13 to recruit B cells via CXCR5.
source: Furthermore, granulomas that form in response to M. tuberculosis often contain follicular dendritic cells which secrete CXCL13 to recruit B cells via CXCR5 (Domingo-Gonzalez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Domingo-Gonzalez et al., 2016).

claim: CCR3 plays a major role in the granuloma response to parasitic Schistosoma mansoni eggs.
source: CCR3, which is expressed mainly by eosinophils, plays a major role in the granuloma response to parasitic Schistosoma mansoni eggs (Chensue, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Chensue, 2013).

claim: Cluster 14 expressed high levels of Cxcl1 but only low levels of Ccl2.
source: For example, cluster 14 (a cluster enriched for hepatocytes) expressed high levels of Cxcl1 but only low levels of Ccl2 (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: Endothelial cell-derived CXCL1 and CXCL2 promote neutrophil exit from the bone marrow.
source: Though a large number of neutrophils are already present in the blood during homeostasis, additional neutrophils expressing CXCR2 exit the bone marrow in response to endothelial cell-derived CXCL1 and CXCL2 (David and Kubes, 2019).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (David and Kubes, 2019).

claim: Tissue-resident macrophages can express CXCL1, CXCL2, and various leukotrienes in response to infection.
source: Furthermore, tissue-resident macrophages can also express CXCL1, CXCL2, and various leukotrienes in response to infection (Soehnlein and Lindbom, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Soehnlein and Lindbom, 2010).

claim: Cxcr2 knockout mice have abnormalities.
source: Though Cxcr2 knockout mice exist, they have abnormalities (Cacalano et al., 1994).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Cacalano et al., 1994).

claim: Monocytes express CXCR2, albeit to a much lesser extent than neutrophils.
source: Because monocytes also express CXCR2, albeit to a much lesser extent than neutrophils, we also stained for CD68.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: There was no marked difference in macrophage numbers in the liver or spleen between PBS- and reparixin-treated mice at 1 DPI.
source: There was no marked difference in macrophage numbers in the liver or spleen between PBS- and reparixin-treated mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H, I.

claim: CCL2 and CCL7 can both bind to CCR2 to induce monocyte trafficking.
source: CCL2 and CCL7 can both bind to CCR2 to induce monocyte trafficking.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about chemokine-receptor interactions.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines and PAMPs can induce CCL2 expression by most cell types.
source: Importantly, pro-inflammatory cytokines and PAMPs can induce CCL2 expression by most cell types (Shi and Pamer, 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Shi and Pamer, 2011).

claim: Deletion of either CCL2 or CCL7 partially diminished monocyte trafficking in response to Listeria monocytogenes infection.
source: Deletion of either ligand partially diminished monocyte trafficking in response to Listeria monocytogenes infection, but the individual role of each ligand was unclear (Jia et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Jia et al., 2008).

claim: Ccr2–/– monocytes are still able to traffic to the site of infection in the spleen during Listeria infection.
source: Lastly, adoptive transfer experiments in the context of Listeria infection showed that Ccr2–/– monocytes are still able to traffic to the site of infection in the spleen (Serbina and Pamer, 2006) and liver (Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Ccr2–/– monocytes are still able to traffic to the site of infection in the liver during Listeria infection.
source: Lastly, adoptive transfer experiments in the context of Listeria infection showed that Ccr2–/– monocytes are still able to traffic to the site of infection in the spleen (Serbina and Pamer, 2006) and liver (Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Excess recruitment of monocytes to M. tuberculosis-induced granulomas leads to increased bacterial replication.
source: Furthermore, excess recruitment of monocytes to M. tuberculosis-induced granulomas leads to increased bacterial replication due to the ability of M. tuberculosis to inhibit degradation within phagosomes in which it resides (Domingo-Gonzalez et al., 2016; Slight and Khader, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: M. tuberculosis can inhibit degradation within phagosomes.
source: Furthermore, excess recruitment of monocytes to M. tuberculosis-induced granulomas leads to increased bacterial replication due to the ability of M. tuberculosis to inhibit degradation within phagosomes in which it resides (Domingo-Gonzalez et al., 2016; Slight and Khader, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Endocytosis of chemokines by endothelial cells helps to diminish chemokine gradients.
source: Under normal circumstances, endocytosis of chemokines by endothelial cells helps to diminish chemokine gradients, limiting prolonged neutrophil recruitment (Kolaczkowska and Kubes, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Kolaczkowska and Kubes, 2013).

claim: Binding to atypical receptors can affect chemokine availability.
source: Furthermore, binding to atypical receptors can also affect chemokine availability, representing another mechanism to resolve inflammation (Hansell et al., 2006; Ulvmar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: MMPs can directly cleave chemokines.
source: MMPs can not only directly cleave chemokines, they can also cleave various chemokine-binding proteins that help establish the chemokine gradient (Parks et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Parks et al., 2004).

claim: MMPs can cleave chemokine-binding proteins that help establish the chemokine gradient.
source: MMPs can not only directly cleave chemokines, they can also cleave various chemokine-binding proteins that help establish the chemokine gradient (Parks et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Parks et al., 2004).

claim: Several studies have found that MMPs can cleave chemokines to alter their function, either increasing or decreasing their receptor binding activity.
source: Several studies have found that MMPs can cleave chemokines to alter their function, either increasing or decreasing their receptor binding activity.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of literature findings.
